Testicular pain

Two sham-controlled trials reported lower pain VAS after PBM in chronic testicular pain, including a distinct post-varicocelectomy cohort. Both papers describe sexual satisfaction as improved, but their numeric satisfaction scores fall and scale anchors are not stated. Each trial enrolled 60 participants and came from the same Iranian research group.

Publications and records

2distinct randomized cohorts

Publication and study types

Human RCT: 2 (n=120 overall)

One post-varicocelectomy trial is also listed in the next row, not a duplicate cohort

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Pain VAS (0–10; mean±SD; active vs sham):
Chronic testicular pain (n=60): 6 weeks, infrared 3.2±0.3, red 3.1±0.9, sham 4.5±0.6; 12 weeks, 2.0±1.0, 1.9±0.4, 3.6±1.4 (both active vs sham p=0.0001).
Post-varicocelectomy orchialgia (n=60): 6 weeks, infrared 3.7±0.3, red 3.6±0.8, sham 4.4±0.6; 12 weeks, 2.1±1.0, 2.1±0.4, 3.3±1.4 (IR vs sham p=0.0001/0.003; red vs sham p=0.0001/0.001).
Both papers say sexual satisfaction improved, but the published means decline and score anchors are absent (Momenzadeh et al., 2024, chronic pain; Momenzadeh et al., 2024, post-varicocelectomy).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate for short-term pain reduction

Very low for sexual-satisfaction effects (VAS direction unclear)

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two sham-controlled trials reported lower pain VAS after PBM in chronic testicular pain, including a distinct post-varicocelectomy cohort. Both papers describe sexual satisfaction as improved, but their numeric satisfaction scores fall and scale anchors are not stated. Each trial enrolled 60 participants and came from the same Iranian research group.

Summary of the Evidence

Two randomized, sham-controlled human trials were identified, with 60 participants in each. One enrolled men with chronic testicular pain and excluded varicocele and previous varicocele surgery. The other enrolled a distinct group with pain after varicocelectomy; it is also listed separately in the following indication row, so that cross-listing is not a third cohort. Both trials came from the same Iranian research group. No animal or in-vitro study of testicular pain was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In the chronic-pain trial, 60 participants were assigned to red laser, near-infrared laser, or sham treatment (20 per group). Pain was measured on a 0–10 visual analogue scale (VAS). Mean pain scores were 3.2±0.3 (infrared), 3.1±0.9 (red), and 4.5±0.6 (sham) at six weeks; at 12 weeks they were 2.0±1.0, 1.9±0.4, and 3.6±1.4, respectively. Active-versus-sham comparisons were reported as p=0.0001 at both follow-ups. The paper also describes sexual satisfaction as improved, but the reported 0–10 satisfaction means fell from 8.1/8.0/8.8 at baseline to 3.9/3.8/5.7 at six weeks and 1.1/1.9/3.8 at 12 weeks (infrared/red/sham). The methods do not define the score anchors or direction, so the numerical changes cannot be interpreted confidently as improvement (Momenzadeh et al., 2024, chronic pain).

The second trial enrolled 60 men with orchialgia after varicocelectomy, again divided into red, infrared, and sham groups of 20. Mean pain VAS scores were 3.7±0.3, 3.6±0.8, and 4.4±0.6 at six weeks, then 2.1±1.0, 2.1±0.4, and 3.3±1.4 at 12 weeks. The reported active-versus-sham p-values were 0.0001 at six weeks, then 0.003 for infrared and 0.001 for red at 12 weeks. The authors also say satisfaction improved, while its reported means decreased from 8.0/8.2/8.9 at baseline to 4.0/3.8/5.4 at six weeks and 1.1/2.0/4.0 at 12 weeks; score anchors are not stated. The cohorts are distinct, but authorship and treatment design were closely related, so independent replication remains important (Momenzadeh et al., 2024, post-varicocelectomy).

Animal evidence

No animal experiment directly testing PBM for testicular pain was identified. Animal studies of testicular injury or hormones were not treated as pain studies.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue study directly assessing testicular pain was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Both trials compared 650-nm red visible light at 50 mW with 820-nm near-infrared light at 100 mW and sham. Treatment was applied bilaterally by probe contact to three points near the upper scrotal nerve, for 15 minutes three times weekly over 12 sessions; exposure was reported as 6–25 J/cm²/day. The protocols used similar wavelengths and schedules but enrolled different patient populations. Because wavelength and output power varied together, the trials do not isolate which parameter accounts for the observed pain changes.

Interpretation

Two small sham-controlled trials from one Iranian research group reported lower short-term pain VAS scores for red and infrared PBM than sham. This supports a low-to-moderate-certainty short-term pain signal, but independent replication and follow-up beyond 12 weeks are lacking. Although both papers call sexual satisfaction improved, their score tables show decreasing values and do not define the VAS anchors; certainty for that outcome is very low. Future trials should prespecify score directions, validate sexual-function measures, recruit across independent centers, and follow participants longer.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two 60-participant sham-controlled trials from one Iranian group reported lower pain VAS through 12 weeks, supporting a short-term pain signal while leaving independent replication and durability uncertain. Both papers also describe improved sexual satisfaction, yet their reported 0–10 satisfaction scores fall sharply without defined scale anchors; the outcome direction cannot be interpreted confidently. Certainty is therefore low-to-moderate for pain and very low for sexual-satisfaction effects.
